store.0: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is really packed, but it's a good kind of busy. I'm finally taking the higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to for a while. It's surreal to be at this stage, because it feels like just yesterday I was in an intro class learning about simple data structures. Now I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. It's exciting to see how far I've come!
store.1: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving. We've been diving into everything from dynamic programming approaches to approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It's really fascinating to see how these concepts can be applied to optimize pathfinding in large networks or handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. Our professor is great at explaining these dizzying concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll put up a problem on the board, something that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time, and then she'll show us a strategy to at least approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with ideas and questions.
store.2: I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course, which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with folks who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas of what the final product should look like. But that's also the beauty of it, right? In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle everything from concurrency issues to node failures gracefully. It's nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a single misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we got that fixed and everything ran smoothly, it was this huge sense of accomplishment.
store.3: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which is a must-take for me since I'm a gamer at heart. The professor is actually from the industry and has worked on a couple of indie games that got some decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, how to implement physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's unbelievably fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.
store.4: I also have an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be too advanced for me. However, the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff and has made me rethink how I approach problems.
store.5: I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It's fancy, but essentially means reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. It's pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major: database management, building an API, front-end interface, plus the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.6: I'm also taking a Philosophy of Mind course, which is my last required non-CS elective. I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it might apply to artificial intelligence. It's a smaller class, so we do a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. Sometimes it's nice to just sit back and analyze abstract ideas. This course also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and it was such a trip to research. I think bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for that perspective.
store.7: My schedule is pretty packed, as you can imagine. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter, with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload.
store.8: The biggest challenge this semester is definitely balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone can eat up ten hours a week, more if we run into a big bug or if the model isn't training properly. Then there's the Distributed Systems project, which is another black hole for time. My group tries to meet at least twice a week, and we rely heavily on Slack or Discord to keep each other updated. Coordinating five different people's schedules is a mini-nightmare, but it's also exciting. This is going to be among my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic, purely about learning, without the pressures of an actual job environment.
store.9: I'm having a blast this semester. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's never as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.
store.10: I'm a fourth-year Computer Science student, and I've seen how the culture has evolved over the years. I've discovered different communities that make this place feel like a second home. There are many ways to get involved beyond just coding in front of your laptop all day.
store.11: I joined the Computer Science Society, which hosts weekly meetups where we discuss new technologies, share personal projects, and have industry speakers. It's a welcoming environment for beginners. I can chat with fellow members who might have worked on similar topics in internships.
store.12: I've been attending the VR/AR Club on and off since my sophomore year. I got hooked when I started doing research in immersive analytics, so it was natural for me to want to hang out with people who share that passion. The club is hands-on—they have a VR lab in the engineering building with headsets, sensors, and quirky prototypes. We host demos where each person shows off their latest project, whether it's a mini-game or something more experimental like AR interfaces for everyday tasks. I love the supportive vibe when people are excited about emerging tech.
store.13: I occasionally pop into the student-run radio station events, like their open-mic nights. People sing, read poetry, or perform stand-up comedy. I remember one night, a friend from the Distributed Systems class performed an acoustic set. He's usually quiet in class, but on stage, he was belting out soulful tunes as if he was born for it. Moments like that remind me there's always more to someone than meets the eye when you're just coding together or doing group projects.
store.14: The campus has these iconic spots, like the central lawn where students hang out between classes. Student organizations set up booths there, and you can see fliers for various clubs. They'll hand out freebies like stickers or candy to attract new members. My weakness is free pizza, so if a club includes that in their ad, I'm easily tempted. The lawn is also where big campus events like Tech Fest take place. During Tech Fest, project teams put up posters, do live demos of their prototypes, and recruiters look for innovative ideas. It's a big deal here, especially for engineering and CS folks.
store.15: I think campus culture is fairly collaborative. There are pockets of competition, especially among seniors trying to land top internships or job offers, but overall, people want to help each other succeed. I remember the campus hackathon in my second year, which was a huge eye-opener. Thousands of students from various backgrounds crammed into the student center for 24 or 36 hours straight, hacking away. It was chaotic but exhilarating. You'd see beginners learning the basics of GitHub while advanced teams used complex machine learning libraries to do real-time image recognition. Sponsors and mentors wandered around to see if anyone needed help. I formed a small team with a few casual acquaintances, and the bond we formed during that all-nighter was unlike anything I'd experienced before. That's the vibe I associate with campus life: you're all in the trenches together, forging friendships through shared experiences and challenges.
store.16: Dorm life can be a huge part of campus culture. In my first two years, I stayed in a dorm specifically for engineering majors, which we jokingly called "The Engi-House." Late-night coding sessions in the common lounge were legendary. Someone would be working on an assignment for Data Structures, while another group might be streaming e-sports tournaments. The environment could get intense at times, with stressed-out engineers fueled by energy drinks. However, it also meant that if you encountered a problem, there was always someone nearby who could provide a quick pointer. Beyond academics, we'd hold potlucks, watch Netflix together, or even host a small talent show to unwind.
store.17: I've been volunteering at outreach events, particularly the "Tech for Good" day organized by our CS department. Local high school students come to campus to learn about programming and problem-solving. I help run mini-workshops on topics like web development or basic Python. It's rewarding to see younger students light up when they create a simple game or animated webpage. I remember how I felt at that age, feeling overwhelmed by the tech world. Giving them a positive first experience is something I take pride in. Events like that show a different side of campus: it's not just about academic research or class assignments; it's about engaging with the community and inspiring the next generation to get excited about STEM fields.
store.18: We have a lively social scene beyond academics. Greek life is an option for those interested, but I didn't join a fraternity. Instead, I found that specialized clubs are a great way to meet like-minded people. For example, a friend who's into robotics joined the Robotics Team and found a second family there. They now hang out on weekends, watch movies together, and grab dinner. I've also formed close bonds with folks in the VR/AR Club and the CS Society. We don't just talk about tech when we're together; we joke around, complain about cafeteria food, or plan weekend trips to the local hiking trails.
store.19: Senior Week is a staple of campus culture, and I'm about to experience it for the first time this year. It's a series of events leading up to graduation, including a formal dance, a carnival, and a day where seniors get pictures taken in their caps and gowns around iconic campus landmarks. I've heard it's bittersweet because it's the last hurrah before everyone scatters. My older pals who graduated last year said it was one of the best weeks of their college life, filled with laughter, nostalgia, and a bit of that sinking feeling that the journey's almost over. I'm excited and a little anxious for it. I've been here for four years, made so many memories, and it's weird to think about not being a student anymore.
store.20: The Rivalry Game is a big campus tradition. Our sports teams face off against our biggest rival college in various sports. I'm not a huge sports fan, but I love the energy on campus that week. People wear school colors, paint their faces, and carry banners. Sometimes, there's a massive pep rally the night before the football game, complete with fireworks. It's a spectacle. Even if you don't attend the game, the campus vibe is electric. Friends gather in dorm lounges or local bars to watch and cheer. If we win, the celebrations last all weekend. If we lose, we still find ways to commiserate together. It's a unifying moment for everyone, from business majors to art students to us nerdy engineers.
store.21: Our school's e-sports team has gained official recognition, and it's awesome to see a broader definition of competition and community. The arena has a wide seating area and a big screen for streaming live competitions. During tournaments, you'll see a hundred or more students gathering to cheer on our team for League of Legends or Overwatch matches. It's great to see e-sports becoming a legitimate campus institution. I never would've guessed it would be this popular when I started college, but times are changing.
store.22: The "Midnight Breakfast" event during finals week is a huge morale booster. It's a bit ridiculous, but it's a great way to remind students that they're not alone in feeling anxious about final exams. Professors serve food, the school band might perform, and everyone takes a break from cramming. It's a small thing, but it does wonders to bring some fun and camaraderie to high-pressure times. I really appreciate the campus culture for making an effort to ensure students have a bit of enjoyment during those stressful periods.
store.23: I think campus life here is what you make of it. If you're willing to explore, approach new people, and join clubs, you'll find a million ways to enrich your experience. It's easy to get lost in your workload, especially in a demanding major like Computer Science, but I've found that attending events, volunteering, and connecting with various communities has been incredibly rewarding. When I look back on my four years, I'll remember the late-night coding, sure, but also the silly game nights in the dorm, the Tech Fest presentations, the hackathon adrenaline, and the excited cheers at the Rivalry Game. It's been a whirlwind, but I wouldn't trade it for anything. Let me know if you ever want a quick tour—I'd be happy to show you some of my favorite spots and introduce you to a few clubs. There's something for everyone here, and I'm so glad I finally embraced all the campus has to offer.
store.24: I'm a fourth-year Computer Science major, and I'm 21, almost 22. My schedule can get hectic with classes and projects, but my hobbies help me stay sane. I love coding, but I also enjoy other activities that give me a break and help me come back to programming with a fresh perspective.

store.27: I've always been fascinated by the idea of exploring new places, and that's something I've tried to do whenever my schedule allows. Since I'm a fourth-year Computer Science major, I have to be pretty strategic about planning my trips—between classes, research, campus clubs, and even everyday stuff like heading to the gym or working on group projects, my calendar gets ridiculously cramped. But I've managed to squeeze in some adventures that have given me some of my favorite memories so far.
store.28: Traveling has become one of those passions I'll keep nurturing even after graduation. I'm anxious to see where my future career in computer science will lead me—I hope to land a job that allows some remote work days or flexible scheduling, so I can keep exploring. Whether it's a weekend trip to a mountain range a few hours away or a flight to a completely different continent, I'm all in. If I ever get the chance to combine my love of coding with my love of travel—like working abroad for a stint or collaborating on an international project—I'd jump at the chance. For now, I'm just enjoying planning the next journey in my head whenever I need a mental break from debugging code. It keeps me motivated, and it's a huge part of why I'm super pumped for the next phase of my life.
store.29: I've been here for four years, and I always say that as much as I love studying computer science, the people I've met along the way are what really keep me grounded and happy.
store.30: I was nervous about whether I'd fit in when I first arrived on campus, but over time, I ended up forming these really tight bonds that have made all the stresses and workload of being a CS major feel way more manageable.
store.31: I guess I should start with my roommate and best friend from freshman year, Tony. We didn't know each other before that first semester, but we clicked right away over this random conversation about a piece of software I was trying to prototype for an Intro to Programming class project. Tony's not even a CS major—he's in mechanical engineering—but we would bounce ideas off each other late into the night, and we realized we had more in common than we initially thought. We both love working with our hands, albeit in different ways: I love to code and design logic, while he loves building things physically. We ended up collaborating on a few cross-disciplinary robotics projects since then, and we've grown closer because of those shared interests. Tony's someone I can always call when I'm overwhelmed with an assignment or if I just want to grab a pizza after a long day.
store.32: I also have a couple of friends I met through the campus sailing club. You wouldn't believe how many CS students I found there—turns out we like to decompress by hitting the water. It creates this fun mix of personalities: we all share an inclination for problem-solving, so we sometimes treat sailing strategy like a puzzle. The camaraderie on the boat is unlike anything else I've experienced in other clubs. You really have to trust each other out on the water. Our team meets at odd hours(often early in the morning) to catch the best conditions, so we really rely on each other to stay motivated. It's a different kind of bond—there's a deep mutual respect because we see each other's strengths and vulnerabilities in such a high-stakes environment. There's no better feeling than looking across the sailboat and seeing your friend flash you a thumbs-up when you maneuver a particularly tricky tack. One friend, Mariah, has ended up becoming a close confidante for me. She was the one who encouraged me last year to apply for a more challenging research position in data science, telling me I should believe in my skills the way she believed in me. That's the kind of unwavering support we have for each other.
store.33: Of course, as a fourth-year, I've also made plenty of connections through my computer science classes—study groups, group projects, or just the random folks I always saw in the lab at two in the morning, trying to debug code the night before a big assignment. There's this sense of solidarity that comes from those late-night coding sessions—like we're going through the trenches together. I vividly remember this one time in my sophomore year, there was a particularly infamously difficult systems programming course. Our final project was basically building a mini operating system kernel from scratch, and we were all losing our minds with memory management bugs. That's actually how I became tight with Carla, another CS major. We ended up bonding over pizza at 3 a.m. because we were the only two left in the lab so late. Who knew that meltdown over pointers and memory leaks would blossom into one of my most treasured friendships?
store.34: Now, I also have some pretty good friends from the gym. Working out has always been an escape for me—I mentioned before that I love to blow off steam by lifting or doing cardio whenever I have a heavy workload. Over time, I kept seeing the same group of people in the early mornings, and it kind of turned into this friendly circle. One of those guys, Dean, is a fellow computer science major, but he's more into machine learning and hardware acceleration projects. He and I started talking shop between sets, which led to us comparing notes on our classes, which then led to us being gym buddies who share nutritional tips, workout regimens—pretty much everything. Now, every so often, we'll game together, too. He's the one who got me hooked on a new co-op adventure game, so it's not just about the gym lifts anymore. It's become a friendship built around mutual support—pushing each other to be better in multiple areas of life.
store.35: Speaking of gaming, that's another circle of friends that's quite dear to me. I'm not a hardcore gamer, but I do spend a decent chunk of time on weekends playing multiplayer strategy games, especially when I need a mental break from writing code or reading research papers. We have this informal e-sports club that meets in a common lounge in our student center. I don't always go, but whenever I do, it's guaranteed quality time with friends. There's something special about gaming with a group in the same room—plenty of laughs, random inside jokes, that collective groan when a team fight goes south, and the ultimate hype when we pull off a last-second victory. Actually, I made a great friend, Derek, through that group—he's super skilled in networking security, and he taught me a bunch of techniques that later proved useful in a cybersecurity research project. And the best part is how naturally our friendship evolved—initially from a shared hobby, and later we just kept supporting each other academically.
store.36: I should also mention that sometimes friendships can come from the most unexpected places—like the campus library. I spend a fair amount of time there when I want a quieter space to study. You can imagine how loaded my schedule can be as a fourth-year CS major: I'm juggling advanced courses, an intense research project, plus some extracurricular commitments. So the library is often my go-to for a peaceful environment. Over the years, I've bumped into the same faces in the same corner desks. One of those people is Jackson, a law student who somehow ended up reading case studies right next to my stack of cryptography textbooks. We started chatting during water breaks, comparing our respective workloads. Over time, we realized we shared an interest in debates—oddly enough, he loves analyzing political and ethical implications of new technologies, so I'd talk to him all day about algorithmic bias. We discovered that, even though we come from different disciplines, we both care about how technology intersects with society's legal structures. Our friendship is more intellectual than some of my others, but it's one I truly value because it broadens my perspective beyond code and servers.
store.37: It's not just about the academic or hobby-driven friendships, though. I've made great friends in unexpected, everyday-life situations, like in the dorm laundry room or while waiting in line for coffee. There was this one day when I was super stressed with a research deadline. I was up too late the night before, so I rushed to the campus cafe half-asleep, waiting in a long line. I started complaining—under my breath, but loud enough for the person behind me to hear—about how I needed more time for my research code to run. Turns out, she was also in the thick of her own mechanical engineering lab fiasco. We commiserated, shared a laugh, and ended up sitting together for coffee. That day, we bonded so much over academic stress that we exchanged contact info, and now, whenever we see each other on campus, we make a point to catch up. She might not be a 'best friend' in the sense of constant hangouts, but it's still a positive, supportive relationship that started organically.
store.38: I think what unites all these friendships is mutual respect and the sense that we're all navigating this crazy journey together. Sometimes, people have this caricature of computer science majors as being antisocial or always stuck behind a screen, but truthfully, my experience has been the opposite. We form these deep connections, especially because the workload and pressure can be so high at times. We're in labs critiquing each other's code, or we're on Slack until the crack of dawn throwing out Hail Mary solutions to some bug—and those challenges bond us. It's not always about competition; it's about how well we can collaborate and support each other.
store.39: Now, as a fourth-year, graduation is looming, and that means a lot of goodbyes eventually. I'm excited about the future—internships, job prospects, maybe grad school. But I can't lie: I'm also dreading the day when all these friends I've made scatter to different corners of the world. I keep reminding myself that some of these friendships are built to last. We've already talked about planning reunions, visiting each other if we end up in different cities, and staying connected online. It's weird thinking how we'll be grown adults in different jobs, possibly different time zones, but hopefully still able to maintain the bond we forged here.
store.40: In some ways, I think that's what real friendship is: you may not always be geographically close, but you have this strong sense of trust, loyalty, and empathy that can transcend distance. I learned that from Tony, who's interning across the country this semester, yet we still FaceTime regularly. I see the same dedication in others as well—like Carla, who's applying to master's programs abroad. We promised that if either of us ends up in Europe, the other has to come visit.
store.41: So yeah, I'm extremely grateful for the friendships I've made through sailing, the gym, gaming, research, random campus encounters—everything. They're truly an integral part of my college experience, and they remind me that there's more to this journey than racking up achievements on my resume. If I log off Zoom or finish a lab feeling like I can call these people my friends... that's what success really looks like to me. And I know that no matter where I end up in my career, I'll carry a piece of each of these friends with me. Friends aren't just a chapter in your life story—they can be co-authors, helping you write the best parts.
